taxonomy.subtopic: High V/Q units and increased alveolar dead space

questions.stem_html: A 52-year-old woman develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 5 days after hip replacement. Arterial blood gas analysis shows hypoxemia and a low PCO2. The accompanying schematic shows an alveolar unit supplied by an obstructed pulmonary arterial branch. Which change occurs in that unit?

options.text_html: Alveolar ventilation ceases while perfusion remains intact
The ventilation-perfusion ratio approaches zero, creating an anatomic right-to-left shunt
The ventilation-perfusion ratio approaches infinity, increasing alveolar dead space
Perfusion exceeds ventilation, causing alveolar carbon dioxide to rise toward mixed venous values
Ventilation and perfusion both increase proportionally, preserving gas exchange

questions.explanation_html: A pulmonary embolus reduces or eliminates perfusion to ventilated alveoli. In the affected region, the V/Q ratio becomes very high and can approach infinity, which increases alveolar and physiologic dead space. Hypoxemia in pulmonary embolism reflects global V/Q mismatch and redistribution of blood flow; hyperventilation commonly lowers arterial PCO2.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: A V/Q ratio approaching zero describes perfused but unventilated alveoli, as in a physiologic shunt.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Perfusion falls abruptly in the obstructed vascular territory.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Ventilation exceeds perfusion in the affected unit; alveolar gas trends toward inspired-air composition.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Pulmonary embolism primarily blocks perfusion, not ventilation.

questions.educational_objective: Pulmonary embolism creates ventilated but underperfused alveoli with a high V/Q ratio and increased physiologic dead space.

media.alt_text: Alveolar-capillary schematic showing preserved ventilation but absent perfusion distal to a pulmonary arterial embolus, with V/Q approaching infinity.
